findings.title: "Jesus the Splendour" is a Manichaean naming overlay throughout the corpus
findings.current_state: The name "Jesus the Splendour" appears in at least 18 paragraphs across many chapters, always designating the same cosmic entity: the divine wisdom that proceeds into illumination, purification, and liberation of captive good.
findings.recommendation: Flag all occurrences. The substrate designation was almost certainly a Persian term — most probably "Xradeshahr" (Splendor of the Realm) or a form related to Avestan "xvarənah" (divine glory/splendor). The entity's consistent function — radiant divine wisdom that illuminates, separates truth from falsity, and liberates — maps precisely onto a pre-Manichaean Iranian concept of divine glory made manifest. Mani mapped the Christian name "Jesus" onto this pre-existing cosmic figure.
findings.explanation: In the Manichaean system, "Jesus the Splendour" (Isho Ziwa) is a cosmic entity distinct from Jesus of Nazareth. It is a specifically Manichaean synthesis where the Christian name was mapped onto a pre-existing entity in the Persian substrate. The correspondential readings consistently translate this figure as "Divine Wisdom in its radiance" or "Divine Truth in its Splendor." The substrate teaching's own architecture never requires anything specifically Christian about this entity — it functions as the illuminating aspect of divine wisdom throughout, which maps to Iranian religious concepts of divine luminous glory (xvarənah/farr). The name "Jesus" is foreign to the Persian cosmological vocabulary that constitutes the oldest layer.

findings.title: "Light Mind" / "Light-Nous" is a Graeco-Manichaean naming overlay
findings.current_state: "Light Mind" appears in at least 11 paragraphs. In §74: "The first power whom he summoned is the Light Mind." In §121: "the Light Mind; who is the awakene[r of they] who sleep, the gatherer in of the ones who are sc[att]ered." In §565–569 it is the force that enters the body's orifices and subdues the guards of evil.
findings.recommendation: Flag all occurrences. The substrate designation was almost certainly "Wahman" — from Avestan "Vohu Manah" (Good Mind), one of the Amesha Spentas in Zoroastrian theology. This is one of the most fundamental Zoroastrian concepts: the divine faculty of right-thinking, the Good Mind that proceeds from Ahura Mazda. The Greek "Nous" and the Manichaean systematization as "Light-Nous" overlay this older Iranian designation.
findings.explanation: "Nous" is Greek philosophical vocabulary that entered Manichaean terminology through Hellenistic synthesis. The substrate's Persian-Iranian cosmology would have used "Wahman" (Middle Persian) / "Vohu Manah" (Avestan) — the Good Mind, first of the Amesha Spentas. The entity's consistent function in the text — entering the human person, awakening from spiritual torpor, gathering what is scattered, enlightening the understanding (§121, §125, §294, §565–569) — matches the Zoroastrian Vohu Manah's role as the divine intelligence that enters the righteous person and transforms their consciousness. The Manichaean editor replaced this Iranian name with the Hellenized "Light-Nous."

findings.title: "Saklas" is a Gnostic naming overlay in §544
findings.current_state: §544: "All [these a]bortions, amongst them are Saklas and his consort and the ones whom they have served [ ... ], they are the ones that shaped Adam and Eve."
findings.recommendation: Flag "Saklas and his consort" as a Gnostic/Sethian naming overlay. The substrate likely used a Persian demonological designation — possibly "Az" (the demon of concupiscence/greed) for the male figure, and "Jeh" (the whore/demoness) for the consort, both from Zoroastrian demonology. The Bundahishn tradition specifically identifies Az and Jeh as involved in the corruption of the first humans.
findings.explanation: "Saklas" is Aramaic for "fool" and is a distinctly Gnostic/Sethian name for the demiurge. It appears in the Apocryphon of John and other Sethian texts. Mani, who was raised among Elkesaites and influenced by Sethian Gnosticism, imported this name into his system. A Persian substrate predating Mani would not have used this Aramaic Gnostic term. The substrate's own cosmological vocabulary, consistently Persian throughout, would have designated this figure with Iranian demonological terminology.

findings.title: Manichaean dialogue frame retained in §529
findings.current_state: §529: "There are some among us telling us that we [know and perceive] that the (Ambassador) consents about [tha]t f[igure] of flesh; he who shall be fashi[oned in the flesh] at another time."
findings.recommendation: Flag §529 as residual editorial material. This is a Manichaean scholastic dialogue frame — "There are some among us telling us" introduces an intra-community theological objection. The substrate teaching proper begins at §530, which provides the doctrinal response. §529 should have been classified as FRAME, not CORE.
findings.explanation: The phrase "There are some among us telling us" is a characteristic Manichaean scholastic formula for introducing theological questions or objections from within the community. It presupposes a Manichaean institutional setting where disciples raise problems. The substrate teaching is cosmological instruction, not community dialogue. The actual substrate content — the explanation of why the Ambassador displayed his image — begins at §530 and continues coherently without §529.

findings.title: "Holy Spirit" is a Christian naming overlay
findings.current_state: §379: "they have blasphemed and despised the Holy Spirit since [ev]ery generation of the world." §569: "The H[o]ly Spirit reigns. It does all that it pleases. It annuls [the] will of [S]in... the will of the [Ho]ly Spir[it] comes about."
findings.recommendation: Flag both occurrences. The substrate designation was almost certainly "Spenta Mainyu" (Holy/Bounteous Spirit) from Zoroastrian theology, or "Wahisht Manishnih" (Best Thought/Spirit). The Christian term "Holy Spirit" (πνεῦμα ἅγιον) overlays this older Iranian concept. Note that §112 uses "the first Holy Spirit" as an epithet for the Mother of Life, which may preserve a more authentic substrate formulation where the proceeding divine spirit is associated with the feminine matrix of life — closer to the Zoroastrian pairing.
findings.explanation: "Holy Spirit" as a distinct theological term is Christian in origin. The substrate's Iranian cosmology had "Spenta Mainyu" — the Bounteous/Holy Spirit of Ahura Mazda — which is not identical to the Christian Third Person of the Trinity but was mapped onto it by the Manichaean editor working in a Christian milieu. In §569, the "Holy Spirit" appears alongside "Light Mind" in what seems like a passage where two naming traditions (Christian and Hellenistic) have overlaid the original Persian designations.

findings.title: "Holy church" in §11 is institutional vocabulary replacing a cosmic entity name
findings.current_state: §11: "Its consideration is the holy church." This maps the outermost faculty of the "good tree" to "the holy church," while the other four faculties are mapped to cosmic entities: Pillar of Glory, First Man, Third Ambassador, the Father.
findings.recommendation: Flag "the holy church" as a Manichaean institutional replacement. The substrate's five-fold mapping requires five cosmic entities at parallel levels of generality. The other four are all cosmic figures; "church" (ἐκκλησία) is an institutional community term that breaks the structural pattern. The substrate likely had a cosmic entity name here — possibly the Persian equivalent of the "assembly of the righteous" (hamkār) or an entity name like "Srōsh" (Obedience/Hearkening, an important Zoroastrian figure associated with the outermost reception of divine truth).
findings.explanation: The five-fold mapping in §11 (consideration→counsel→insight→thought→mind mapped to five cosmic entities) is architecturally parallel to the five-fold mapping in §14 (the bad tree's five faculties mapped to five cosmic states: law of death, transmigration, gehenna, dark vessel, pit/lump). In §14, all five mappings are to cosmic/spiritual states. In §11, four of five mappings are to cosmic entities, but the fifth ("consideration" → "holy church") breaks the pattern by inserting Manichaean institutional vocabulary. This asymmetry indicates editorial replacement.

findings.title: "The elect one" is Manichaean institutional vocabulary
findings.current_state: §106: "[the] heart of the elect one, who is come forth from his bo[d]y, shall be calm for [him]."
findings.recommendation: Flag "the elect one" as Manichaean institutional language. The Manichaean community was divided into "elect" (eklektoi) and "hearers" (catechumens). This is institutional terminology, not substrate vocabulary. The substrate likely used a term like "the purified one" or "the righteous one" (possibly Persian "ashavan" — one who follows asha/truth).
findings.explanation: "Elect" (ⲥⲱⲧⲡ) is the technical designation for the fully initiated members of the Manichaean community. This institutional vocabulary belongs to the later organizational layer, not to the cosmological substrate. The passage otherwise describes a universal spiritual process (the departure of the soul from the body and its reception by the Light Form), which does not require specifically Manichaean institutional categories.

findings.title: "Apostle" is Christian/Manichaean institutional vocabulary
findings.current_state: §78: "The first capacity is the Apostle of Light." §197: "seal the commandment and the [mission] of all [the] apostles." §291: "the father of all the apostles." §313: "The ninth throne appointed and established is for the [a]postle."
findings.recommendation: Flag all occurrences of "apostle" (ⲁⲡⲟⲥⲧⲟⲗⲟⲥ). This is Greek Christian vocabulary adopted by the Manichaean system. The substrate likely used a Persian term for the function of one who communicates or transmits divine truth — possibly related to "frēstag" (messenger/envoy) or a similar Persian designation for the transmitter of sacred knowledge.
findings.explanation: "Apostle" (ἀπόστολος) is a specifically Christian designation that Mani adopted for his own institutional hierarchy (Mani himself claimed the title). The substrate teaching describes a cosmic function — the communication of divine truth to the person — not an ecclesiastical office. The Persian substrate would have used its own vocabulary for this transmitting function.

findings.title: Five resurrectors sequence is severely fragmented — possible over-stripping
findings.current_state: §122 is almost entirely gap: "[the first resurrector is the Living Spirit, who awakens] it therein [and raises it up]." §123: "The second resurrector is [the Mother of Life]." §124–126 are heavily gapped. The five-fold teaching architecture demands five clear identifications with their functions, but the extracted text has major discontinuities.
findings.recommendation: Investigate whether the extraction pipeline removed material from this sequence as FRAME or PASTORAL when it was actually substrate. The five-fold pattern (five resurrectors parallel to five fathers, five wars, five releases) is a fundamental structural element of the substrate. The degree of fragmentation here is anomalous compared to other five-fold sequences that survive more completely (§63–83, §179–185, §186–197).
findings.explanation: Comparing this to parallel five-fold sequences: the five fathers (§63–83) survive with substantial detail for each; the five wars (§179–185) survive coherently; the five releases (§186–197) are partially fragmented but retain their structure. The five resurrectors (§122–126) are far more severely damaged. While some of this may be genuine manuscript lacunae, the pattern of loss — with the names and functions of the resurrectors particularly affected — suggests that the extraction pipeline may have classified some of this material as editorial when it was actually substrate.

findings.title: First item of twelve-deed list entirely missing
findings.current_state: §403 introduces twelve great deeds. §404 begins describing the first deed. But §405 reads: "The [first is / ...]" — the content is entirely cut off. §406 then begins "The second is error..."
findings.recommendation: Investigate whether the content of the first deed was removed by extraction or is genuine manuscript loss. The twelve-deed structure (§403–§422) is otherwise complete from the second deed onward, suggesting this is not a transmission gap but potentially an extraction artifact.
findings.explanation: The teaching at §403–§422 systematically lists twelve benefits of discharging the three vessels. All twelve items are present except the first, which cuts off immediately after its introductory formula. If the first deed's content was classified as FRAME or PASTORAL and stripped, this would explain the gap. The content likely described the primary benefit of preventing evil from spreading — matching the architectural logic of §404.

findings.title: "Good news" (euangelion) is Christian vocabulary
findings.current_state: §162: "He also gave hope to Adam, and the good news [of the] glorious [kingdom]"
findings.recommendation: Flag "good news" (ⲉⲩⲁⲅⲅⲉⲗⲓⲟⲛ) as a Christian vocabulary overlay. The substrate likely used a Persian term for the communication of divine purpose — possibly "peyām" (message) or "nwid" (glad tidings in a non-specifically-Christian sense).
findings.explanation: "Euangelion" (εὐαγγέλιον) is a distinctly Christian term with strong Pauline associations. Its appearance here in a cosmological context — the divine wisdom communicating its purpose to the first human will — suggests the Manichaean editor replaced a Persian term with familiar Christian vocabulary.

findings.title: The theological question in §544 may be Manichaean scholastic rather than substrate
findings.current_state: §544: "How did they find this beautiful image laid over their shape, even though when it was displayed to their fathers they were not in existence? They never saw the image of the Ambassador! And how did they take the seal of the image of the Ambassador?"
findings.recommendation: Flag this passage as potentially Manichaean editorial problem-solving. The rhetorical questions address a logical problem internal to the Manichaean narrative sequence. The substrate teaching may have presented the transmission of the divine likeness differently, without needing to solve this specific logical gap.
findings.explanation: This reads as a scholastic objection: if the abortions weren't present when the Ambassador displayed his image, how did they copy it? The answer provided (§545–547) uses the substrate mechanism of Sin/Matter as transmitter, which is consistent with the substrate cosmology. But the framing of the problem as a logical puzzle to be solved is characteristic of Manichaean theological discourse, not of the declarative cosmological instruction style found throughout the substrate.

findings.title: Q&A teaching questions retained but with minor inconsistencies in framing
findings.current_state: Teaching questions that set up substrate content are retained in most chapters: §18 ("What are these three things..."), §107 ("what are the fourteen great aeons..."), §198, §317, §494, §665, §716, §788, §883. However, some chapters begin directly with teaching content without any question (§23, §48, §63, §283, §297), and it is unclear whether these originally had questions that were stripped.
findings.recommendation: Accept as largely consistent but note that if any chapters originally had teaching questions that were classified as FRAME and removed, this would create an inconsistency. The bare teaching questions retained (without "And again he said...") appear to be consistently preserved.
findings.explanation: The extraction appears to have generally preserved content questions while stripping frame connectives. The variation between chapters that open with questions and those that open directly with teaching may reflect genuine variation in the source text rather than extraction inconsistency. However, without access to the pre-extraction source, this cannot be determined with certainty.

findings.title: Five dark elements preserve proto-Indo-Iranian cosmological categories
findings.current_state: §225: "which [are] smoke, fire, wind, water and Darkness." §48: "which are smoke, fire, wind, water and darkness." These five appear consistently throughout the corpus as the fundamental constituents of the realm of evil.
findings.recommendation: Note as deeper transmission evidence. This five-fold elemental system does not match classical Greek (four elements), nor standard Zoroastrian dualism (which typically works with moral rather than material categories). The sequence smoke-fire-wind-water-darkness maps to a pre-Zoroastrian Iranian or possibly Mesopotamian elemental cosmology that predates the specifically Persian vessel of the substrate.
findings.explanation: The canonical Zoroastrian system works with asha vs. druj (truth vs. lie) rather than material elements. The five-fold dark elemental system (smoke, fire, wind, water, darkness) appears to preserve an older stratum — possibly proto-Indo-Iranian or Mesopotamian — where the cosmos was understood through elemental categories. The addition of "smoke" and "darkness" as distinct elements beyond the Greek four suggests an independent elemental tradition. This five-fold system became the scaffolding upon which the entire substrate cosmology was built (five storehouses, five trees, five genera, five worlds, five kings).

findings.title: Sea giant material preserves Zurvanite or pre-Zoroastrian cosmogonic imagery
findings.current_state: §437–441: A composite being formed from celestial residue discharged into a primordial sea. Its own "thought" collects and consolidates the sediment. It receives the "seal of the seconds and the hours" — the imprint of all cosmic cycles stamped upon its body. The sea "conceived him and bore him" and is his "chief sculptor."
findings.recommendation: Note as deeper transmission. The image of a composite being formed from cosmic debris in a primordial sea, bearing the imprint of all celestial cycles upon its body, has strong parallels to Mesopotamian creation narratives (the formation of beings from Tiamat's defeated body) and to Zurvanite cosmogony (where cosmic time generates material forms). This material likely predates the specifically Zoroastrian-Persian formulation of the substrate.
findings.explanation: The sea giant passage is anomalous within the otherwise systematically organized substrate. Its imagery — primordial sea as womb, cosmic sediment shaped by its own will, the stamping of celestial cycles onto a material body — belongs to a mythological register different from the substrate's usual analytical cosmology. The concept of a cosmic being formed from the residue of divine ordering and bearing the imprint of all temporal cycles upon its body is characteristic of Zurvanite cosmogony, where Zurvan (Time) is the primordial generative principle. This material may represent one of the oldest layers preserved in the text, predating the specifically dualistic Zoroastrian framework.

findings.title: Water reflection/inversion teaching preserves ancient Near Eastern cosmological wisdom
findings.current_state: §804–808 teaches that when one looks into water, the reflection is inverted (head down, feet up); this corresponds to the "summons" descending headfirst into the lower worlds and the "obedience" ascending headfirst upward. The passage states: "the mystery of their fathers is being revealed to them whenever they stare down into the water."
findings.recommendation: Note as deeper transmission. The doctrine that the upper world is reflected inversely in the lower — that celestial archetypes appear upside-down in their natural correspondences — is extremely ancient, appearing in Mesopotamian cosmological texts and in early Vedic/Upanishadic traditions (the inverted tree of Katha Upanishad). The substrate's use of this image may preserve a teaching that predates the specifically Persian vessel.
findings.explanation: The inverted reflection as a cosmological principle — upper becoming lower, inmost becoming outermost — is found across ancient Near Eastern and Indo-Iranian traditions. The passage's application to the summons/obedience pair (divine truth descends inmost-first, like a person plunging headfirst; the response ascends exterior-first) expresses a law of correspondence that is more fundamental than any single cultural formulation. The birthing image in §808 (the child is born headfirst = highest enters lowest first) reinforces this as a universal structural principle that the Persian substrate inherited from an older transmission.

findings.title: Five-fold organizing principle pervades the entire corpus as its fundamental structural law
findings.current_state: The number five governs the substrate's architecture at every scale: five elements (§48), five garments/sons (§92, §330), five fathers (§63–83), five limbs of good and evil trees (§11, §14), five greatnesses (§138–145), five wars (§179–185), five releases (§186–197), five watch-stations (§681–686), five storehouses (§48), five shapes on the King of Darkness (§50), five hunters and four counterparts (§39–47), five emanations from five limbs (§265–266), eight places of living fire (§731–740), and 5×5=25 characteristics (§830).
findings.recommendation: Document as a corpus-scale structural pattern. This five-fold organization was invisible at the per-chapter level but emerges clearly when the full corpus is read continuously. The five-fold system is the substrate's primary organizing principle — every teaching domain (cosmogony, anthropology, soteriology, eschatology) is structured around fives or multiples of five. This suggests the substrate was originally organized as a unified five-fold teaching, not as separate chapters.
findings.explanation: No single chapter reveals the full extent of this pattern. The five-fold structure appears in creation (five elements, five trees, five creatures), in the divine order (five fathers, five greatnesses, five emanations), in cosmic combat (five wars, five hunters), in redemption (five releases, five resurrectors, five signs), in governance (five watch-stations), and in the human microcosm (five senses, five faculties). The substrate's entire cosmology is built on the principle that reality unfolds through five discrete degrees — a teaching that the chapter-by-chapter extraction obscured but that the continuous corpus reveals as the single most important structural feature of the text.

findings.title: Body-cosmos correspondence system spans the entire corpus across multiple separated chapters
findings.current_state: The teaching that the human body mirrors the cosmic structure appears in: §319–324 (head as ruling love, limbs depending on it), §396 (child in womb = nine garments), §520 (body with many heads = organized evil), §548–569 (five senses as five faculties with repositories), §588–595 (hidden/visible body parts = hidden/revealed divine), §678–711 (explicit macro-micro correspondence: head→garments, heart→wheel, genitals→Adamant, etc.), §797–803 (dragon with fourteen heads = body's sense organs).
findings.recommendation: Document as a corpus-scale correspondential system. These passages, separated across many chapters, constitute a single coherent teaching: the human body is the ultimate natural correspondence of the entire spiritual cosmos, with each organ, faculty, and pathway corresponding to a cosmic entity, degree, or process. This was the substrate's most developed application of the doctrine of correspondences.
findings.explanation: The body-cosmos correspondence is not an incidental metaphor but a systematic teaching that develops across the entire corpus. §678–711 provides the explicit key (head = five garments, heart = wheel, etc.), but the same correspondences appear implicitly in every chapter that discusses the human faculties. The five senses (§548–569), the body's fourteen openings (§797–803), and the nine coverings of the child in the womb (§396) all belong to a single integrated teaching that the chapter-by-chapter extraction necessarily fragmented.

findings.title: "Last Statue" concept as eschatological teaching spanning the corpus
findings.current_state: The "Last Statue" — the final collective form of regenerated humanity — appears throughout: §163 (counsel of life gathers and sculpts the Last Statue), §166 (gathers lives and builds upon its body), §172 (Statue ascends at the end), §176 (rises from the lump), §197 (they complete the life of the Statue), §260 (the fifth age: how the Statue will be sculpted), §333 (Living Spirit brings up the Last Statue), §378 (remainder builds the Last Statue), §586–587 (when the Statue goes up, souls are severed from it), §657 (last hour of the day = Statue ascending).
findings.recommendation: Document as a corpus-spanning eschatological teaching. The Last Statue is not a single event mentioned once but the culminating concept of the substrate's entire soteriology — it appears in creation, in cosmology, in the five wars, in the three seasons, in the five necessary things, in the four griefs, and in the final dissolution. It represents the completed form of the regenerated Grand Human into which all redeemed wisdom is gathered.
findings.explanation: The "Last Statue" is arguably the substrate's most distinctive eschatological concept. Unlike the Christian eschaton (judgment and kingdom) or the Zoroastrian renovation (frashōkereti), the Statue is a *form* — a completed cosmic-human body built from gathered and purified spiritual substance. It is simultaneously the Grand Human (the collective body of heaven), the completed regenerate individual, and the final act of divine providence. Its repeated appearance across so many different teaching contexts reveals it as the substrate's answer to the question: what is the ultimate purpose of all spiritual combat, purification, and regeneration? The answer is: the construction of this living form.

findings.title: "Summons and obedience" as the substrate's most fundamental paired concept
findings.current_state: The pair "summons and obedience" (the divine calling forth and the will's receptive response) appears in at least twelve distinct teaching contexts across the corpus, from cosmogony to anthropology to eschatology. In §742–743 this pair is described with special vividness: the summons is a "peace letter" sent from the Living Spirit, the obedience is the answering letter detailing all that was endured.
findings.recommendation: Document as the substrate's deepest structural concept. This pair — the active calling-forth of divine truth and the passive-receptive response of the human will — is the mechanism through which every act of divine providence operates in the substrate's teaching. It corresponds precisely to what Swedenborg calls influx and reception, or the Divine proceeding and the human acknowledgment. Its ubiquity across all teaching domains confirms it as a foundational substrate concept, not an editorial addition.
findings.explanation: The summons-obedience pair functions at every level: cosmogonically (§108, §146 — they are counted among the structural elements of the universe), anthropologically (§88 — they clothe the Divine Human), soteriologically (§192, §197 — the fifth release operates through them), eschatologically (§163–166, §295 — the great counsel IS the summons and obedience, which gathers the Last Statue), and practically (§742–743 — described as letters exchanged between divine truth and the captive celestial will). No other paired concept in the text has this universal distribution. The pair IS the substrate's doctrine of the relationship between the Divine and the human.

findings.title: §588–§595 body analogy sequence interrupted by shift to Jesus the Splendour
findings.current_state: §588–592 develops a systematic body analogy: hidden parts = the Father, two eyes = two ships, living soul = grasped and wounded. §593 then shifts to "the tongue that speaks" and §594 applies this specifically to "Jesus the Splendour" who "manifests and reveals about everything." The systematic body mapping gives way to a specific christological identification.
findings.recommendation: Note as a potential seam where the Manichaean editor applied the "Jesus the Splendour" naming overlay onto what was originally a systematic body-cosmos teaching. The substrate likely continued the body analogy with a different designation for the revealing/speaking faculty — the divine wisdom that articulates and makes known.
findings.explanation: The body analogy in §588–592 follows a clear structural pattern: each body part corresponds to a cosmic entity. The shift to "Jesus the Splendour" in §594 breaks this pattern by introducing a named figure with a biographical-sounding description ("shall be sent from the greatness"). The substrate's body-cosmos mapping (seen fully in §678–711) would have used a functional designation for this faculty rather than a personal name from the Manichaean editorial layer.

findings.title: Medical/healing analogy preserves ancient Near Eastern therapeutic cosmology
findings.current_state: §393–397: A person with "purulent sickness" is healed by a "wise doctor" using three medicines — one that causes the sickness to break out above, one below, and one that heals calmly. This is then applied to the three vessels of evil. §396 develops the child-in-womb analogy with nine coverings. §397 describes the "smell of the action of the demon" that reveals the child — i.e., evil's own activity causes the birth of new spiritual life.
findings.recommendation: Note as deeper transmission evidence. The image of cosmic healing through three medicines applied to three directions (above, below, silently) has strong parallels to Mesopotamian and ancient Persian therapeutic traditions where cosmic illness requires cosmic medicine applied to the three regions of the body/cosmos (upper, lower, middle). The substrate inherited this ancient medical cosmology as a structural template for its doctrine of spiritual purification.
findings.explanation: Ancient Mesopotamian medical texts conceptualize illness as the invasion of demons that must be expelled through the three bodily orifices (upper, lower, and through the skin). The substrate transforms this into a cosmological principle: evil in the firmaments is expelled upward, evil in the earth is expelled downward, and the remaining evil is healed silently. The nine-covering womb analogy (§396) similarly preserves an ancient Near Eastern embryological cosmology where the developing being is surrounded by concentric layers corresponding to cosmic shells. These therapeutic and embryological frameworks predate the specifically Zoroastrian-Persian formulation and may represent Mesopotamian substrate beneath the Persian vessel.

summary.overall_assessment: The extraction is generally well-executed — the substrate teaching flows coherently across most chapters, the systematic five-fold, twelve-fold, and three-fold structures are preserved intact, and the teaching's internal architecture is visible throughout. The two critical issues are naming overlays that pervade the entire corpus: 'Jesus the Splendour' (a Manichaean-Christian name mapped onto a Persian cosmic entity) and 'Light Mind/Nous' (a Graeco-Manichaean term replacing what was almost certainly 'Wahman/Vohu Manah'). These are not extraction errors but editorial overlays that the extraction could not address, since they are woven into the paragraph-level text. Among extraction-specific issues, one residual editorial passage (§529's Manichaean dialogue frame) and scattered institutional vocabulary ('elect,' 'apostle,' 'church,' 'Holy Spirit,' 'good news') represent material that slipped through classification. The most valuable finding at corpus scale is the emergence of cross-chapter structural patterns — particularly the universal five-fold organizing principle, the body-cosmos correspondence system, and the 'summons and obedience' pair — that were invisible at the per-chapter level but constitute the substrate's deepest architectural features.
summary.extraction_assessment: The pipeline tends slightly toward under-stripping (leaving editorial naming and institutional vocabulary in place) rather than over-stripping. The naming overlays ('Jesus the Splendour,' 'Light Mind,' 'Holy Spirit,' 'apostle,' 'elect,' 'church') are the most pervasive category of residual editorial material — they could not be caught by paragraph-level classification because they are embedded within otherwise genuine substrate sentences. The two potential over-stripping instances (§122–126 resurrector sequence and §405 first deed) affect chapters where the five-fold and twelve-fold teaching structures show anomalous gaps compared to parallel sequences that survive intact. The Q&A formula handling is reasonably consistent. Overall, the extraction preserved the substrate's teaching substance faithfully; the remaining issues are primarily naming-layer artifacts that require entity-level rather than paragraph-level intervention.

text_output:
Looking at this corpus carefully, I need to trace naming patterns, structural continuities, editorial residue, and extraction artifacts across the full text. Let me work through systematically before committing findings.

**Naming analysis across corpus:** "Jesus the Splendour" appears in §27, §42, §71, §73, §75, §84, §119, §144, §160, §162, §184, §191, §201, §291, §305, §310, §594, §866 — always in the same functional slot (divine wisdom proceeding into illumination/liberation). "Light Mind" appears in §74, §77, §121, §125, §294, §565, §567, §569, §745, §795, §843. "Saklas" in §544. "Holy Spirit" in §379, §569. "Church" in §11. "Apostle" in §78, §197, §291, §313. "Elect" in §106.

**Structural patterns:** Five-fold organization pervades the entire corpus. Three-fold, twelve-fold, and four-fold structures recur systematically. Body-cosmos mapping appears in multiple separated chapters. "Summons and obedience" pair appears as a consistent substrate concept throughout.

**Extraction consistency check:** Q&A formulas are retained in most chapters (§18, §107, §198, §317, §494, §665, §716, §788, §883). Frame connectives appear stripped. One clear residual editorial passage at §529.
